overview: After Morocco’s invasion of Songhay in 1591, surviving rulers established an independent government downstream in Dendi. Their history belongs beside that of the diverse Niger River communities, rather than a single unchanging state. The imported 1878 to 1900 outline lies much too far north, in the Sahara; it does not locate historical Dendi reliably.

periods.title: Songhay government survives downstream
periods.summary: The Moroccan conquest displaced part of Songhay’s ruling class into Dendi.

periods.title: River communities and competing authorities
periods.summary: Later documents describe several local centers; French treaties reached Gaya in 1895 and Karimama in 1897.

periods.title: Colonial division and continued communities
periods.summary: Colonial rule divided the river region, while its languages and communities endured.

sections.title: A successor state and a wider region

items.text: The Moroccan victory in 1591 ended the great Songhay Empire’s earlier supremacy. Some members of its ruling class moved down the Niger and continued an independent government. Dendi therefore belongs to the history of survival and political rebuilding after imperial defeat.

Late Dendi cannot safely be drawn as one permanent kingdom. Documents cited in Niger’s 2004 court submission include separate French treaties with Gaya in 1895 and Karimama in 1897. These records show several centers of authority; the submission itself was arguing a contested boundary case.

sections.title: Homes and food before the kingdom

items.text: Birnin Lafiya reveals an older Dendi landscape, occupied approximately from the fourth to thirteenth centuries. Excavators found a compound with circular rooms, rammed-earth walls and a partially enclosed courtyard. This predates the post-1591 successor kingdom by centuries.

Some floors were paved with broken pottery; others used laterite. A potsherd-covered step led into one room. An old pot could become part of the floor beneath your feet: the excavated surfaces show how carefully ordinary spaces were constructed.

Plant and animal remains at Birnin Lafiya include pearl millet, African rice, cotton and many floodplain fish. Charcoal also points to useful fruit trees, including shea. The household food supply drew on both cultivated land and the river.

Reassembled vessels include large containers, probably for storage or liquids, and burnished bowls likely used for food and drink. Archaeologists also recovered glass, stone and shell beads. Kitchen equipment and small ornaments help populate a history otherwise dominated by rulers.

Dendi-speaking commercial neighborhoods also developed farther south in Borgu towns such as Parakou, Djougou and Kandi. Farias argues that these trading communities may predate the migration after 1591. Speaking a related language did not mean belonging to one kingdom.

In these commercial centers, Dendi also served people whose first languages were different. A shared trading language helped customers, travelers and hosts communicate. Its continued use is one of the region’s achievements that cannot be measured by the size of a royal army.

A short written sample is “Dèndí cínè”, meaning “the Dendi language”, as printed in Farias’s 2013 study. This is modern scholarly Latin transcription, with tone marks. It represents the living language, rather than a claimed quotation from a seventeenth-century royal manuscript.

Kompanti’s foundation traditions, recorded in 2013, describe families leaving Boyeri after warfare involving Kandi late in the nineteenth century. Researchers recorded Gulmanceba and Fulani neighborhoods, including people whose ancestors had escaped dependence elsewhere. Community history preserves refuge and rebuilding as well as battles.

sections.title: How ordinary lives enter the record

items.text: The Kompanti interviews named cultivators Tchayenu Dagu and Sibo Hamani and former weaver Sido Alfari. Such witnesses link family memory with practical knowledge of land and work. Their accounts were collected in 2013, not treated as untouched recordings from the nineteenth century.

A small 2014 excavation at Kompanti recovered pottery fragments, a glass bead and a cowrie fragment. Its shallow deposits were consistent with a relatively recent settlement. Comparing material remains with oral histories lets researchers test a story instead of simply choosing whichever version sounds grandest.

ending.text: French conquest and colonial administration curtailed the region’s independent authorities around the turn of the twentieth century. The map’s 1900 endpoint is not a securely established single fall date for every Dendi community. River settlements, trading connections and Dendi speech continued across the new administrative divisions.
